claims.claim: The page walks the full route a bill takes from introduction to presidential action
claims.sourceSpan: A bill (or other item of business) may travel through a series of steps in the legislative process—from introduction to committee and floor consideration to possible presidential consideration.

claims.claim: The page is checked against House Rules XV and XX, 1 U.S.C. 106-107, the Congressional Budget Act and Article I, and covers the routes to the floor that bypass the Rules Committee
claims.sourceSpan: a committee from consideration of a public bill or public resolution that has been referred to it for 30 legislative days

claims.claim: CRS states that the process by which a bill becomes law is rarely predictable and that for many bills it will not follow the usual sequence
claims.sourceSpan: the process by which a bill can become law is rarely predictable and can vary significantly from bill to bill. In fact, for many bills, the process will not follow the sequence of congressional stages that are often understood to make up the legislative process.

claims.claim: A House bill is introduced by electronic submission or by dropping it in the hopper, a wooden box on the House floor
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, a bill is introduced when it is submitted electronically or dropped in the hopper (a wooden box on the House floor).

claims.claim: In the Senate a bill is submitted to clerks on the Senate floor
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, the bill is submitted to clerks on the Senate floor.

claims.claim: A measure takes a designation based on its chamber of introduction, for example H.R. or H.J.Res. for House-originated bills
claims.sourceSpan: the bill will receive a designation based on the chamber of introduction, for example, H.R. or H.J.Res. for House-origi

claims.claim: S. 1884, the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025, became Public Law 119-82 on April 13, 2026
The 119th Congress has issued 102 public laws so far, through Public Law 119-102
Committees receive far more referrals than they can pursue and do not formally consider each referred bill
claims.sourceSpan: Each committee receives many bill referrals over the course of a Congress—far more than the panel is capable of pursuing in any detail.

claims.claim: Committees do not formally consider each referred bill
claims.sourceSpan: Committees do not formally consider each of these referred bills.

claims.claim: A bill is typically referred to the committee or committees with jurisdiction over its elements
claims.sourceSpan: it is typically referred to the committee (or committees) in that chamber with jurisdiction over its elements

claims.claim: On a multiple referral one committee is designated the primary committee of jurisdiction
claims.sourceSpan: One of those committees will be designated the primary committee of jurisdiction and will likely take the lead on any action that may occur.

claims.claim: In the Senate, in almost all cases a bill is referred to only the committee with jurisdiction over the issue that predominates in it
claims.sourceSpan: in almost all cases, the bill is referred to only the committee with jurisdiction over the issue that predominates in the bill.

claims.claim: The committee chair holds the chief agenda-setting authority for the committee
claims.sourceSpan: The committee's chair has the chief agenda-setting authority for the committ

claims.claim: Clause 2 of House Rule XV lets a member file a motion to discharge a committee from a bill referred to it for 30 legislative days
claims.sourceSpan: A Member may present to the Clerk a motion in writing to discharge--

claims.claim: The discharge motion reaches a committee that has held a public bill or resolution for 30 legislative days
claims.sourceSpan: (A) a committee from consideration of a public bill or public resolution that has been referred to it for 30 legislative days

claims.claim: A majority of the total membership of the House means 218 members, per Speaker Byrns in 1936
claims.sourceSpan: The phrase ``a majority of the total membership of the House'' was construed to mean 218 Members (Speaker Byrns, Apr. 15, 1936, p. 5509)

claims.claim: Once signed by a majority of the total membership the motion is entered on the Journal, published with its signatories, and referred to the Calendar of Motions to Discharge Committees
claims.sourceSpan: House shall have signed the motion, it shall be entered on the Journal, published with the signatories thereto in the Record, and referred to the Calendar of Motions to Discharge Committees.

claims.claim: A committee may conduct hearings so members and the public can hear from selected parties about a bill
claims.sourceSpan: A committee may conduct hearings on a bill to provide committee members and the public an opportunity to hear from selected parties (e.g., a federal agency or organized interest) about the bill's strengths and weaknesses.

claims.claim: A committee that wants to recommend a bill to its chamber holds a markup, at which members vote on proposed amendments
claims.sourceSpan: If the committee wants to formally recommend that the bill receive consideration from its parent chamber, it will hold a markup on the bill, at which committee members vote on any proposed amendments.

claims.claim: A reported bill is often accompanied by a committee report explaining the provisions and the changes the committee recommends
claims.sourceSpan: it is often accompanied by a committee report, a document that explains the provisions in the bill and any changes recommended by the committee

claims.claim: Some judges treat committee reports as stronger evidence of Congress’s understanding of a law than individual floor statements from non-sponsors
claims.sourceSpan: Some judges have suggested certain forms of legislative history are more reliable than others, with committee reports providing stronger evidence of Congress’s understanding of the law than individual floor statements from non-sponsors, for example.

claims.claim: House majority party leaders generally decide which bills receive floor consideration, either scheduling streamlined consideration or asking the Rules Committee for tailored parameters
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, majority party leaders generally decide which bills will receive floor consideration; typically, they schedule a bill for a type of streamlined floor consideration, or instead ask the Rules Committee to propose a set of tailored parameters for floor consideration.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: In the House most bills that receive consideration do so under suspension of the rules, with 40 minutes of debate, no floor amendments, and a two-thirds vote of Members voting
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, most bills that receive consideration do so under a procedure called "suspension of the rules," which limits debate to 40 minutes and prohibits floor amendments, but requires two-thirds of Members voting to agree.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: Most other bills are considered under parameters set by a special rule reported by the House Rules Committee, which often operates as an arm of the majority party leadership
claims.sourceSpan: Most other bills are considered under tailored debate and amending parameters set by the terms of a special rule reported by the House Rules Committee (which often operates as an arm of the majority party leadership).
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: A bill need not be reported from committee before the House can consider it under suspension
claims.sourceSpan: There is no requirement that a bill must be reported from committee before the House can consider it under suspension.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: The discharge motion also reaches the Committee on Rules, on a resolution held for seven legislative days that proposes a special order of business
claims.sourceSpan: (B) the Committee on Rules from consideration of a resolution that has been referred to it for seven legislative days and that proposes a special order of business for the consideration of a public bill or public resolution that has been reported by a committee or has been referred to a committee for 30 legislative days.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: Senate bills reach the floor only on a motion to proceed, typically by the majority leader, or by unanimous consent
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, bills are brought to the floor only after the Senate agrees to a motion (typically offered by the majority leader) to proceed to a specific bill or, alternatively, if no Senator objects to a unanimous consent request to bring it up.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: A special rule is a simple House resolution adopted case by case, usually carrying the text to be considered, a period for general debate and limits on floor amendments
claims.sourceSpan: The House establishes these parameters on a case-by-case basis through the adoption of a simple House resolution (an H. Res.) called a special rule.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: The common provisions found in a special rule are the text to be considered, a period for general debate and limits on floor amendments
claims.sourceSpan: Common provisions found in a special rule include the identification of the text to be considered, a specified period for general debate, and limits on the amendments that can be offered on the floor.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: A special rule may place few restrictions on amending, but typically allows only specified predetermined amendments or precludes floor amendments altogether
claims.sourceSpan: The committee could report a special rule that places few restrictions at all on amending. Typically, however, the special rule will allow only specified predetermined amendments to be offered or may instead preclude floor amendments altogether.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: The Rules Committee generally operates as an arm of the majority party leadership, with majority members outnumbering minority members nine to four
claims.sourceSpan: This committee generally operates as an arm of the majority party leadership, and majority party members outnumber minority party members, nine to four.
claims.section: Step 5: Scheduling and the Rules Committee

claims.claim: Committees are not limited to measures referred to them and may initiate legislative action on their own
claims.sourceSpan: Committees are not limited, however, to consideration of measures referred to them and may initiate legislative action on their own.

claims.claim: The House considers the special rule itself for approximately one hour and proceeds to the bill only after adopting it
claims.sourceSpan: the House first considers that special rule itself on the House floor, for approximately one hour. After debate, the House votes on adopting the special rule;

claims.claim: A cloture motion is signed by at least 16 Senators, voted on two days of session later, and if three-fifths agree further consideration is limited to 30 hours
claims.sourceSpan: can file a cloture motion, signed by at least 16 Senators. Two days of session later, Senators vote on the cloture motion. If three-fifths—usually 60 Senators

claims.claim: After debate and amendment the House typically votes on a minority-party motion to recommit before final passage
claims.sourceSpan: the House then typically votes on a motion to recommit offered by a minority party member before proceeding to a final vote on passage

claims.claim: No Senate rule permits a numerical majority to end debate on most questions, so senators may wage a filibuster
claims.sourceSpan: A defining feature of Senate floor consideration is that no rule permits a numerical majority to end debate and proceed to a final vote on most questions (e.g., a bill or amendment). Thus, Senators may wage a filibuster, effectively threatening extended debate or other actions that would delay or prevent a final vote.

claims.claim: Senate Rule XXII closes debate on a vote of three-fifths of the Senators duly chosen and sworn, except on a measure or motion to amend the Senate rules
claims.sourceSpan: decided in the affirmative by three-fifths of the Senators duly chosen and sworn--except on a measure or motion to amend the Senate rules, in which case the necessary affirmative vote shall be two- thirds of the Senators present and voting

claims.claim: The cloture machinery is not the Senate’s only route: frequently the Senate puts aside the formal rules and agrees by unanimous consent to tailored parameters on debate and amending
claims.sourceSpan: frequently the Senate decides it can more effectively act by putting aside the formal rules and instead agreeing—by unanimous consent—to tailored parameters on debate and amending.

claims.claim: Much of Senate business is conducted by unanimous consent, in which a measure passes so long as no senator objects
claims.sourceSpan: much of Senate business is conducted by unanimous consent, in which a measure passes so long as no senator objects

claims.claim: A House recorded vote is ordered on a request supported by at least one-fifth of a quorum
claims.sourceSpan: that request is supported by at least one-fifth of a quorum

claims.claim: In a full House a recorded vote is ordered by 44, and in the Committee of the Whole by 25 under clause 6(e) of Rule XVIII
claims.sourceSpan: In a full House (total membership of 435), a recorded vote is ordered by one-fifth of a quorum (44), but in the Committee of the Whole a recorded vote is ordered by 25 (clause 6(e) of rule XVIII)

claims.claim: Clause 2(a) of Rule XX sets the minimum time for a record vote or quorum call by electronic device at 15 minutes
claims.sourceSpan: the minimum time for a record vote or quorum call by electronic device shall be 15 minutes

claims.claim: Clause 9(a) lets the Speaker reduce the minimum electronic voting time to not less than two minutes on a question following another electronic vote
claims.sourceSpan: The Speaker may reduce to not less than two minutes the minimum time for electronic voting on any question that follows another electronic vote or a report from the Committee of the Whole

claims.claim: Senate Rule XII provides that when the yeas and nays are ordered the names of Senators are called alphabetically and each declares assent or dissent without debate
claims.sourceSpan: When the yeas and nays are ordered, the names of Senators shall be called alphabetically; and each Senator shall, without debate, declare his assent or dissent to the question

claims.claim: The Senate takes a roll-call vote if one-fifth of a quorum of senators request it
claims.sourceSpan: If one-fifth of a quorum of senators request it, the Senate will take a roll-call vote.

claims.claim: In a Senate voice vote the names of the senators and the tally of votes are not recorded
claims.sourceSpan: In a voice vote, the names of the senators and the tally of votes are not recorded.

claims.claim: One chamber frequently agrees to the other chamber’s bill without changes, but sometimes proposes changes
claims.sourceSpan: One chamber frequently agrees to a bill—without changes—that was sent to it by the other, but sometimes a chamber proposes changes to a bill sent to it by the other.

claims.claim: Amendments between the houses is a back-and-forth trading of proposals, also called amendment exchange or ping-pong
claims.sourceSpan: is called amendments between the houses (or amendment exchange, or sometimes simply ping-pong)

claims.claim: For a bill to have a chance of becoming law one chamber must eventually agree to the proposal the other sent it
claims.sourceSpan: For the bill to have a chance of becoming law, one chamber must eventually agree to the proposal that the other chamber sent it.

claims.claim: Differences may instead be resolved through a conference committee whose compromise is embodied in a conference report
claims.sourceSpan: Sometimes, the resolution of differences between the House and Senate proposals may instead be accomplished through a conference committee.

claims.claim: Conferees are drawn primarily from the standing committees with jurisdiction over the bill
claims.sourceSpan: drawn primarily from the standing committee(s) with jurisdiction over the bill

claims.claim: A conference report may be considered under the same procedures used for other business but cannot be amended
claims.sourceSpan: the conference report may be considered under the same procedures used for other business, though it cannot be amended

claims.claim: When a bill passes either House it is printed and that printed copy is called the engrossed bill
claims.sourceSpan: when such bill or resolution passes either House, be printed, and such printed copy shall be called the engrossed bill

claims.claim: The engrossed bill is signed by the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate and sent to the other House
claims.sourceSpan: Said engrossed bill or resolution shall be signed by the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate, and shall be sent to the other House

claims.claim: The enrolled bill is signed by the presiding officers of both Houses and sent to the President
claims.sourceSpan: it shall be printed and shall then be called the enrolled bill, or joint resolution, as the case may be, and shall be signed by the presiding officers of both Houses and sent to the President of the United States

claims.claim: Enrolled bills are printed on parchment or paper of suitable quality as determined by the Joint Committee on Printing
claims.sourceSpan: Enrolled bills and resolutions of either House of Congress shall be printed on parchment or paper of suitable quality as shall be determined by the Joint Committee on Printing.

claims.claim: The 1990 waiver of sections 106 and 107 covers any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill or continuing resolution of that Congress
claims.sourceSpan: of any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill, or continuing resolution of the One Hundred First Congress

claims.claim: If the President approves a bill he shall sign it
claims.sourceSpan: If he approve he shall sign it

claims.claim: A vetoed bill is returned with objections to the originating chamber, which enters them on its Journal and reconsiders
claims.sourceSpan: he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated, who shall enter the Objections at large on their Journal, and proceed to reconsider it

claims.claim: Override votes must be taken by yeas and nays with the names entered on each chamber’s Journal
claims.sourceSpan: in all such Cases the Votes of both Houses shall be determined by yeas and Nays, and the Names of the Persons voting for and against the Bill shall be entered on the Journal of each House respectively

claims.claim: Successful overrides of presidential vetoes are rare
claims.sourceSpan: Successful overrides of presidential vetoes are rare

claims.claim: A bill not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, becomes law as if signed
claims.sourceSpan: If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it

claims.claim: The exception is that if Congress by their adjournment prevent the bill’s return, it shall not be a law
claims.sourceSpan: unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law

claims.claim: Reconciliation limits Senate debate time, which means cloture and its three-fifths vote is not necessary to reach final passage
claims.sourceSpan: A distinctive feature of reconciliation is that debate time is limited in the Senate, which means cloture (and its requisite three-fifths majority vote) is not necessary to reach a vote on final passage.

claims.claim: 2 U.S.C. 641(e)(2) limits debate in the Senate on a reconciliation bill, and all amendments and debatable motions and appeals in connection with it, to not more than 20 hours
claims.sourceSpan: Debate in the Senate on any reconciliation bill reported under subsection (b), and all amendments thereto and debatable motions and appeals in connection therewith, shall be limited to not more than 20 hours.

claims.claim: There are three types of reconciliation directives: spending, revenues and the public debt limit
claims.sourceSpan: There are three types of reconciliation directives: to change laws providing for spending, to change laws providing for revenues, and to change the public debt limit.

claims.claim: No more than one reconciliation bill may respond to each type of instruction in one budget resolution, for a maximum of three reconciliation bills
claims.sourceSpan: No more than one reconciliation bill may include provisions in response to each type of instruction in one budget resolution, for a maximum of three reconciliation bills.

claims.claim: In practice Congress has generally combined the reconciliation submissions into a single omnibus measure
claims.sourceSpan: In practice, Congress has generally combined the reconciliation submissions from every committee into a single, omnibus reconciliation measure.

claims.claim: The Byrd rule is section 313 of the Budget Act and prohibits extraneous matter in a reconciliation bill
claims.sourceSpan: most notably Section 313 of the Budget Act, known as the Senate's Byrd rule

claims.claim: 2 U.S.C. 644 makes a provision extraneous if it produces changes in outlays or revenues merely incidental to the non-budgetary components of the provision
claims.sourceSpan: a provision shall be considered extraneous if it produces changes in outlays or revenues which are merely incidental to the non-budgetary components of the provision

claims.claim: 2 U.S.C. 641(g) bars a reconciliation bill containing recommendations with respect to the old-age, survivors, and disability insurance program under title II of the Social Security Act
claims.sourceSpan: that contains recommendations with respect to the old-age, survivors, and disability insurance program established under title II of the Social Security Act

claims.sourceSpan: Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 P.L. 111-152

claims.sourceSpan: the FY2018 reconciliation law (P.L. 115-97), sometimes referred to as the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act

claims.sourceSpan: The short titles for some reconciliation measures were omitted or struck pursuant to points of order and are referred to by other means.

claims.claim: The extent to which subcommittees play a formal role varies by chamber and by committee tradition and practice
claims.sourceSpan: The extent to which subcommittees play a formal role in policymaking—for example, by holding hearings or marking up legislation prior to full committee consideration—varies by chamber and by committee tradition and practice.

claims.claim: Subcommittees cannot report legislation to the chamber; only full committees may do so
claims.sourceSpan: Whatever role a full committee allows its subcommittees to play, subcommittees cannot report legislation to the chamber; only full committees may do so.

claims.sourceSpan: provisions increasing or waiving (for a temporary period or otherwise) the public debt limit under section 3101(b) of title 31, United States Code

claims.claim: Reconciliation is a two-phase process whose first phase is the adoption of a budget resolution
claims.sourceSpan: Reconciliation is a two-phase process. In the first phase, the House and Senate adopt a budget resolution

claims.claim: Two of the four content points of order apply in both the House and the Senate
claims.sourceSpan: These points of order apply in both the House and the Senate:

claims.claim: Section 310(d) prohibits amendments to reconciliation legislation that would cause a net increase in the deficit for the years covered by the instruction
claims.sourceSpan: Amendments to reconciliation legislation cannot increase the deficit. Section 310(d) prohibits the consideration of amendments to reconciliation legislation that would cause a net increase in the deficit for the fiscal years covered by the reconciliation instruction.

claims.claim: Section 310(g) prohibits consideration of reconciliation legislation recommending changes to Title II of the Social Security Act
claims.sourceSpan: Reconciliation legislation cannot amend the Social Security program. Section 310(g) prohibits the consideration of reconciliation legislation that recommends changes to Title II of the Social Security Act (the retirement, survivors, and disability programs).

claims.claim: The other two content points of order apply in the Senate only
claims.sourceSpan: These points of order apply in the Senate only:

claims.claim: Section 313, the Byrd rule, prohibits matter extraneous to the instructions to a committee
claims.sourceSpan: Matter in reconciliation legislation cannot be extraneous. Section 313, also known as the Byrd rule, 7 prohibits the inclusion of matter in a reconciliation measure that is "extraneous to the instructions to a committee.

claims.claim: Section 310(e) requires amendments to reconciliation legislation to be germane, which the standing rules of the Senate do not generally require of amendments
claims.sourceSpan: Amendments to reconciliation legislation must be germane . In general, the standing rules of the Senate do not impose subject matter limitations on amendments to legislation.

claims.sourceSpan: The enrollment of any such bill or joint resolution shall be in such form as the Committee on House Administration of the House of Representatives certifies to be a true enrollment.

claims.claim: The 1990 waiver has the Clerk of the House prepare a printed enrollment after enactment, as in the ordinary case
claims.sourceSpan: the Clerk of the House of Representatives shall prepare a printed enrollment of the bill or joint resolution as in the case of a bill or joint resolution to which sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code, apply.

claims.claim: A 1995 waiver reached a debt limit extension measure as well
claims.sourceSpan: A debt limit extension measure.

claims.claim: REMOVED: "describes a process that happens for maybe 5% of enacted legislation. The other 95% takes routes that the civics class doesn’t cover." The opening sentence of the site’s largest explainer, and an invented statistic: no stored source contains it, and a search of the whole data/ref-text corpus for 5%/95%/5 percent/95 percent returns nothing relevant. Replaced with what CRS actually says about how unpredictable the route is.
claims.sourceSpan: the process by which a bill can become law is rarely predictable and can vary significantly from bill to bill

claims.claim: REMOVED: "Of the roughly 15,000 to 20,000 bills introduced each Congress, approximately 300 to 600 typically become law." No stored source contains either range. Replaced with the CRS statement about referral volume and with the real, sourced public-law count for this Congress. NOTE for a later batch: articles/what-is-a-committee.html carries a DIFFERENT uncited version of the same statistic and was not edited here.

REMOVED: "No discharge petition or parliamentary maneuver can force a committee to act — the chair’s control is near-absolute during normal legislative business." Clause 2 of House Rule XV establishes exactly that maneuver, and the site’s own discharge-petition explainer documents it. The article now quotes the rule, gives the 218-signature threshold and links the explainer.
claims.sourceSpan: A Member may present to the Clerk a motion in writing to discharge--

claims.claim: REMOVED: "The majority party leadership controls the Rules Committee completely. If the Speaker doesn’t want a bill to come to the floor, it won’t — regardless of how many members support it." Rule XV clause 2(a)(1)(B) makes the Committee on Rules itself dischargeable on the same 218 signatures, and CRS records that most bills reaching the House floor do so under suspension rather than under a special rule. Both are now on the page.
claims.sourceSpan: (B) the Committee on Rules from consideration of a resolution that has been referred to it for seven legislative days

claims.claim: CORRECTED: "It can only be used once per budget resolution." CRS R48444 states the real limit — one bill per type of instruction, for a maximum of three per budget resolution. claims.sourceSpan: for a maximum of three reconciliation bills

claims.claim: SOURCED, NOT REMOVED: the list of laws enacted through reconciliation rested on nothing. CRS R48444 was fetched and stored this session and its Appendix Table A-1 sources every entry, with public law numbers. The FY2025 reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21, July 4, 2025) — a law of the Congress this site tracks — was missing from the list and is now on it. NOTE: articles/budget-reconciliation.html carries a different, shorter list and was not edited here.
claims.sourceSpan: FY2025 reconciliation law e P.L. 119-21 139 Stat 72-401 7/4/2025

claims.claim: CORRECTED: "it cannot change Social Security benefits" understated the bar. 2 U.S.C. 641(g) bars any reconciliation bill containing recommendations with respect to the OASDI program under title II — not only benefit levels.
claims.sourceSpan: that contains recommendations with respect to the old-age, survivors, and disability insurance program

claims.claim: CORRECTED: the article said an enrolled bill is "certified by the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate (depending on which chamber originated the bill)". Under 1 U.S.C. 106 those officers sign the ENGROSSED bill; the ENROLLED bill is signed by the presiding officers of both Houses. Both printings are now described in the right order with the right signers.
claims.sourceSpan: shall be signed by the presiding officers of both Houses and sent to the President of the United States

claims.claim: CORRECTED: "printed on parchment paper" stated one of the statute’s two options as the only one. 1 U.S.C. 107 says parchment or paper of suitable quality, as the Joint Committee on Printing determines.
claims.sourceSpan: shall be printed on parchment or paper of suitable quality as shall be determined by the Joint Committee on Printing

claims.claim: CORRECTED: the hopper was described as "a wooden box near the House clerk’s desk" and as the only route, and Senate introduction as obtaining recognition to introduce a bill verbally. CRS R42843 places the hopper on the House floor, records electronic submission as a current House method, and describes Senate introduction as submission to clerks on the Senate floor. Nothing in the stored set supports the recognition mechanic.
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, a bill is introduced when it is submitted electronically or dropped in the hopper (a wooden box on the House floor).

claims.claim: REMOVED: "Conference committees were common in earlier decades but have become rarer; amendment ping-pong is now the more frequent reconciliation mechanism." CRS R42843 describes both routes and makes no frequency comparison. It also uses the word reconciliation only for the budget process, so the section now uses CRS’s own term — amendments between the houses — and says plainly that this step is not budget reconciliation.
claims.sourceSpan: Sometimes, the resolution of differences between the House and Senate proposals may instead be accomplished through a conference committee.

claims.claim: CORRECTED: "Members have 15 minutes to reach the floor and record their vote" presented a minimum as a fixed window. Rule XX clause 2(a) sets 15 minutes as the minimum, and clause 9(a) lets the Speaker cut it to not less than two minutes.
claims.sourceSpan: The Speaker may reduce to not less than two minutes the minimum time for electronic voting

claims.claim: REMOVED: "the results are publicly available on the House Clerk’s website within minutes of the vote’s conclusion." No stored source addresses publication timing. The sourced part — that the site takes House roll calls from the Clerk — is kept.
claims.sourceSpan: clerk.house.gov/evs/

claims.claim: CORRECTED: "The Senate uses a voice vote for routine matters, and a roll call vote for significant legislation" replaced the rule with a judgment about significance. The Senate takes a roll call if one-fifth of a quorum request it. The article also said senators say "aye" or "nay"; the Senate’s own page says yea and nay.
claims.sourceSpan: If one-fifth of a quorum of senators request it, the Senate will take a roll-call vote.

claims.claim: SOURCED: "a cloture vote (which requires 60 votes to succeed)" and "the Senate filibuster effectively requires 60 votes" cited nothing. Rule XXII in the stored Senate Manual now carries the claim, including the exception in the same sentence — two-thirds present and voting on a measure to amend the Senate rules. The page makes no claim about the 2013/2017/2025 precedents, so it does not carry the nuclear-option defect the sweep found on the Senate-procedure pages.
claims.sourceSpan: decided in the affirmative by three-fifths of the Senators duly chosen and sworn

claims.claim: CORRECTED: the self-descriptive section listed the status indicators as "In Committee," "Passed House," "Passed Senate," "Signed". The code’s label set is Introduced, In Committee, On House Calendar, Passed House, Passed Senate, Signed into Law — two labels were missing and one was wrong.
claims.sourceSpan: label: 'On House Calendar'

claims.claim: REMOVED: the unsourced glosses — "This referral is not ceremonial", the committee chair’s "significant power", the Rules Committee as "the gatekeeper", committee reports being "often the richest source of substantive analysis", "A bill with multiple referrals faces a harder path", and the claim that hearings are "publicly recorded and archived on the committee’s website and through GovInfo", which no stored source supports.
claims.sourceSpan: The committee's chair has the chief agenda-setting authority for the committ

claims.claim: ROUND 1, MY OWN FRESH READ before the hostile pass reported: seven sentences this rewrite had itself introduced were unsourced and are cut or replaced. “The hopper is the detail everyone remembers; electronic submission is the one most descriptions leave out” (a claim about other people’s writing, and the same defect a reviewer had just found on the sibling page); “Most bills introduced in Congress are never enacted” (an unsourced proportion, replaced by the CRS referral-volume statement); “A bill the chair never schedules does not move on the committee’s own initiative” (contradicted by CRS’s own parenthetical, now quoted instead); “this is where the textbook account and the House rules actually diverge”; the closed-rule / open-rule definitions (no stored source defines either term — replaced with CRS’s own description of what a special rule carries, plus the nine-to-four committee ratio); “can differ substantially from the one introduced”; and “The Senate has no direct equivalent to the Rules Committee route” (an unsourced negative).
claims.sourceSpan: Committees are not limited, however, to consideration of measures referred to them and may initiate legislative action on their own.

claims.claim: ROUND 1, my own read: the inherited description of House floor time control (a manager for the majority, the ranking minority member, time yielded in short blocks) rests on nothing in the stored set. Replaced with what CRS states: the special rule carries a specified period for general debate, the House considers the rule itself for about an hour, and it reaches the bill only after adopting it.
claims.sourceSpan: the House first considers that special rule itself on the House floor, for approximately one hour

claims.claim: ROUND 1 FIX, found by my own read before the reviewer reported: the draft said “public law numbers run in order of enactment within a Congress”. The stored list falsifies a strict reading — Public Law 119-68 is dated 2026-02-11 while 119-69 is dated 2026-01-14. The claim is gone; only the count and the range are stated, and both are receiptable.
claims.sourceSpan: Highest public law number: 119-102.

claims.claim: ROUND 1 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass): the draft listed H.Res., S.Con.Res. and S.Res. as designations. Those strings appear ZERO times in the stored CRS report; it gives only H.R./H.J.Res. and S./S.J.Res. The sentence is cut back to what the source says.
claims.sourceSpan: H.R. or H.J.Res. for House-originated bills or joint resolutions and S. or S.J.Res. for Senate-originated measures

claims.claim: ROUND 1 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass): the stage-label list was presented as exhaustive and omitted “On Senate Calendar”, which scripts/lib/stage.js emits for a Senate-origin bill on a calendar. My own earlier grep for label literals missed it because the label sits inside a ternary — a deterministic search agreeing with itself, which is exactly what the genuine-read rule exists for.

claims.claim: ROUND 1 FIX: the page said “for each stage we record the date it was reached”. refresh_stages.js bumps stageDate to the LATEST ACTION DATE on any new activity, including housekeeping actions that advance no stage, because it is the sort key for the bill list. Corrected here and on the legislative-stages draft, which carried the same wrong description.
claims.sourceSpan: bumps stageDate to the latest action date

claims.claim: ROUND 1 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass), the systemic one: SEVEN sources quoted in the body — 1 U.S.C. 106, 2 U.S.C. 641, 2 U.S.C. 644, the Senate Manual, senate.gov About Voting, CRS 98-314 and CRS R45153 — appeared in NEITHER the JSON-LD citation array nor the Key Sources box, and the audit note claiming the citation work was complete was itself wrong. All seven added to both, 1 U.S.C. 107 added to the JSON-LD side, the never-quoted filibusters-cloture page and Congress.gov glossary removed. Both surfaces now carry the same 14 entries. Third instance of this class in one batch and no gate checks it.
claims.sourceSpan: Said engrossed bill or resolution shall be signed by the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate

claims.claim: The citation list and Key Sources box previously named the Congress.gov glossary, the Senate filibuster page, CRS R48444, and the two clerks’ vote pages. CRS R48444 was cited but had never been fetched or stored; it is now both. CRS R42843, the House Rules and Manual, the National Archives Constitution transcript and 1 U.S.C. 107 are added, because they are what this audit read.
claims.sourceSpan: The Reconciliation Process: Frequently Asked Questions

claims.claim: ROUND A FIX (mine, on nobody’s list): the draft said "Two of those go by names that are not their legal titles" and named only P.L. 115-97 and P.L. 117-169. CRS R48444 names FOUR measures whose short titles were omitted or struck, THREE of which are on this article’s own list of enacted reconciliation laws — the third being the FY2025 law, P.L. 119-21, "sometimes referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act", the most recent and most prominent of the set. Corrected to three and every name now quoted from the report.
claims.sourceSpan: the FY2025 reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21), sometimes referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act

claims.claim: ROUND A FIX (mine): the draft said the short titles "were struck by Byrd rule points of order before enactment". R48444 says only "omitted or struck pursuant to points of order" and attributes them to no particular rule. The Byrd-rule attribution and the "before enactment" gloss were the article’s, not the source’s, and are gone. The ledger rows rec.2017 and rec.2022 had carried the same over-claim past their own receipts, which supported only the "sometimes referred to as" naming; both claim texts were corrected too.
claims.sourceSpan: The short titles for some reconciliation measures were omitted or struck pursuant to points of order and are referred to by other means.

claims.claim: ROUND A FIX (mine): the draft said 2 U.S.C. 641(e)(2) "caps debate on a reconciliation bill at not more than 20 hours" without naming the chamber. The subsection is headed "Procedure in Senate" and its text limits "Debate in the Senate". An unscoped reading of this exact limit is the defect already live on articles/budget-reconciliation.html (which invents a per-chamber conference limit), so the sentence now quotes the statute in full and says it binds the Senate.
claims.sourceSpan: Debate in the Senate on any reconciliation bill reported under subsection (b), and all amendments thereto and debatable motions and appeals in connection therewith, shall be limited to not more than 20 hours.

claims.claim: ROUND A FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier): "the chair often sends the bill to a subcommittee first" was an unaudited frequency claim with no ledger row and no source — and CRS says the opposite kind of thing, that subcommittee practice VARIES by chamber and committee. Replaced with the report’s own two sentences, including the limit that subcommittees cannot report legislation to the chamber.
claims.sourceSpan: The extent to which subcommittees play a formal role in policymaking—for example, by holding hearings or marking up legislation prior to full committee consideration—varies by chamber and by committee tradition and practice.

claims.claim: ROUND A, NOT FIXED HERE (out of batch scope): the hostile verifier confirmed two live sibling pages now disagree with this one. articles/budget-reconciliation.html still says "only one reconciliation bill is permitted per budget resolution" (R48444: up to three), omits P.L. 119-21 from its list, and presents "Tax Cuts and Jobs Act" as the law’s title. Flagged for the budget batch; nothing on that page was touched.
claims.sourceSpan: for a maximum of three reconciliation bills

claims.claim: SIGN-OFF ROUND (2026-08-31, hostile Sonnet pass over the frozen file, restricted to the four round-A fixes plus a whole-article sweep): SIGN OFF. All four fixes PASS with source quoted. The arithmetic on "three of those" was independently re-derived: CRS lists FOUR measures with omitted or struck short titles, of which H.R. 3762 was vetoed and never enacted, so exactly three of the article’s seven enacted reconciliation laws are in that set. The 20-hour citation was confirmed to sit in subsection (e), headed "Procedure in Senate", and the pass separately confirmed that nothing else in 2 U.S.C. 641 imposes a House debate limit the new wording could misrepresent.
claims.sourceSpan: Debate in the Senate on any reconciliation bill reported under subsection (b)

claims.claim: SIGN-OFF FIX (minor): "our guide to the discharge petition covers how rarely that threshold is reached" asserted a frequency this article sources nowhere, by deferring it to another page. Reworded to state the question rather than answer it. This is the same unsourced-generality class the round-A subcommittee fix uncovered; a full sweep of every frequency word in the article found no other instance outside a direct quotation.
claims.sourceSpan: The phrase ``a majority of the total membership of the House'' was construed to mean 218 Members

claims.claim: SIGN-OFF FIX (minor, carried across from the legislative-stages pass in the same batch): the enrollment-waiver sentence named only appropriations bills and continuing resolutions. The 1 U.S.C. 106 notes show the waivers also covered reconciliation bills and debt limit extension measures. Enumeration completed and receipted on both pages so the two do not diverge.
claims.sourceSpan: of any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill, or continuing resolution of the One Hundred First Congress presented to the President after the enactment of this joint resolution

claims.claim: SIGN-OFF FIX (minor): "Reconciliation is a two-phase process built on a budget resolution" was verbatim-accurate but carried no ledger row — a coverage gap, not a content error. Row added.
claims.sourceSpan: Reconciliation is a two-phase process. In the first phase, the House and Senate adopt a budget resolution

claims.claim: ROUND D FIX (material, and the sharpest finding of the whole batch): the article said "Two limits do bind the contents" and named the Byrd rule and the Social Security bar. CRS R48444’s own question 5 - in the report the article quotes three sentences later - names FOUR points of order, and sorts them: section 310(d) (no deficit-increasing amendments) and section 310(g) (no Social Security changes) apply in BOTH chambers, while section 313 (the Byrd rule) and section 310(e) (germaneness of amendments) apply in the SENATE ONLY. A precise, falsifiable completeness claim, wrong against the source on the desk. Rewritten to four, with the chamber split, every element receipted.
claims.sourceSpan: Amendments to reconciliation legislation must be germane . In general, the standing rules of the Senate do not impose subject matter limitations on amendments to legislation.

claims.claim: ROUND D FIX (material): "Much of the Senate’s work never reaches that machinery" was the article’s own sentence, and it stacked an absolute on a quantifier that no source states in that form. CRS says only that "frequently the Senate decides it can more effectively act by putting aside the formal rules"; the Senate.gov "much of Senate business" line is about Senate business generally, not about bypassing cloture specifically. Replaced with a transition that asserts only what the two quotes establish: that machinery is not the Senate’s only route.
claims.sourceSpan: frequently the Senate decides it can more effectively act by putting aside the formal rules and instead agreeing—by unanimous consent—to tailored parameters on debate and amending.

claims.claim: ROUND D FIX (minor, three of a kind): "In the Senate a bill usually goes to the single committee", "A reported bill is normally accompanied by a committee report" and "CRS lists what one usually carries" were all frequency words chosen by us rather than by the source. CRS says "in almost all cases" (stronger than usually), "often accompanied" (weaker than normally) and "common provisions found in a special rule include". All three now quote the report.
claims.sourceSpan: in almost all cases, the bill is referred to only the committee with jurisdiction over the issue that predominates in the bill.

claims.claim: ROUND D-ERA FIX (material precision, found in the main thread while adjudicating the sibling article): the draft said Congress waived the printed enrollment "altogether". The 1 U.S.C. 106 notes do not support that: about a dozen waiver provisions run from 1988 to 1999, and only a handful of them - Pub. L. 101-497, Pub. L. 101-466, Pub. L. 100-454, and the FY1988 provisions at Pub. L. 100-203 section 8004 and Pub. L. 100-202 section 101(n) - go on to require a printed enrollment prepared after enactment. The waiver drops the printing before presentment and substitutes a committee-certified hand enrollment; it does not abolish the printed enrollment. One hostile pass called "altogether" accurate and another called it an overclaim; reading the notes settles it against "altogether". CORRECTION TO THIS NOTE: an earlier version named Pub. L. 104-54 and 102-260 among the subsequent-printing provisions. A later hostile sign-off read both in full and found no such clause in either, and re-deriving the clause positions in the stored text confirms it. The list above is the corrected one.
claims.sourceSpan: the Secretary of the Senate shall prepare a printed enrollment of the bill as in the case of a bill to which sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code, apply.

claims.claim: ROUND D, NOT FIXED HERE (out of batch scope, flagged for the budget batch): articles/budget-reconciliation.html contradicts this page on three checkable points - it says "only one reconciliation bill is permitted per budget resolution" (CRS: up to three), it omits P.L. 119-21 and presents "Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017" as P.L. 115-97’s title, and it folds the Social Security bar INTO the Byrd rule when CRS treats them as separate points of order under different sections. Also flagged: articles/discharge-petition.html dates the 218 threshold to 1935 while the House Manual attributes the construction to Speaker Byrns in 1936 - possibly two different facts, but two live pages give two years. Nothing on either page was touched.
claims.sourceSpan: Reconciliation legislation cannot amend the Social Security program. Section 310(g) prohibits the consideration of reconciliation legislation that recommends changes to Title II of the Social Security Act (the retirement, survivors, and disability programs).

claims.claim: CROSS-BATCH FIX (material, handed over by the veto-cluster batch and re-verified here against its stored CRS RL30909): the article said a pocket veto leaves "nothing to override, because there was no return." That REASON is the 1929 Pocket Veto Case dicta, which RL30909 records as "dicta and not the central holding of the case" and which Wright v. United States and Kennedy v. Sampson both cut against. It is also falsified in practice: in 1974 both chambers overrode a claimed pocket veto of the Vocational Rehabilitation Act Amendments (House Nov 20, Senate Nov 21) - the year is 1974, checked against the report because a verifier in the other batch got it wrong once - and the Administration then refused to promulgate it. The sentence now says the question is contested and quotes the report for both points. RL30909 was copied from the veto worktree rather than re-fetched, registered on ref-sources.json and added to this page’s citation list and Key Sources box.
claims.sourceSpan: This latter point, regarding legislative agents, was dicta and not the central holding of the case.

claims.claim: SIGN-OFF FIX (material, third pass over the same sentence): the waiver passage had been rewritten to describe a general practice while quoting a certification clause from one provision and asserting the subsequent printing flatly. A hostile sign-off on the sibling article showed the certification quote comes from a provision that does not cover every class named, and that only 5 of about 13 waiver provisions carry a subsequent-printing clause. Rewritten again to anchor on ONE provision that carries all three elements itself - the 1990 waiver, Pub. L. 101-466: it names reconciliation bills, appropriation bills and continuing resolutions, it carries the House Administration certification, and its section 2 has the Clerk prepare the printed enrollment after enactment. The debt-limit class is now attributed separately to the 1995 waiver, and the U.S. Code’s own note heading for the run is quoted.
claims.sourceSpan: the Clerk of the House of Representatives shall prepare a printed enrollment of the bill or joint resolution as in the case of a bill or joint resolution to which sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code, apply.

claims.claim: FINAL SIGN-OFF FIX (material, fourth pass over the same sentence, and the batch’s clearest lesson): the rewrite had read "The 1990 waiver shows the shape of it". Two independent hostile passes landed on the same objection - one graded it low, the sibling article’s pass REFUSED to sign off - and both were right. "Shows the shape of it" is a representativeness claim whose antecedent is the general practice, and it is not supported: only about five of the roughly dozen waiver provisions, all from 1987-1990, carry a subsequent-printed-enrollment clause, while the more numerous 1992-1999 group stops at the certified hand enrollment. Rewritten so every clause is attributed to a named, dated provision and nothing is claimed about the practice beyond "repeatedly waived both sections outright". The two October 1990 waivers are now disambiguated by date, and the 1995 provision’s own certifying committee is named rather than left to inherit the 1990 one.
claims.sourceSpan: shall be in such form as the Committee on House Oversight of the House of Representatives certifies to be a true enrollment.

claims.claim: FINAL SIGN-OFF FIX (minor): the Ford paragraph said Congress "treated them as ordinary returns" without saying how that was procedurally possible against a claimed pocket veto. RL30909 supplies the mechanism - a protective return, where the President claims the pocket veto and returns the bill anyway - and the sentence now carries it. Completeness, not a correction.
claims.sourceSpan: the President claims the power of pocket veto but, at the same time, returns the bill to Congress for a possible override.

claims.claim: FINAL CONFIRMATION ROUND (2026-08-31): a hostile Sonnet pass read the third rewrite of the enrollment-waiver passage in BOTH articles at once, having been told exactly why the two earlier versions were refused. Verdict: SIGN OFF on both. It confirmed every fragment verbatim, that all three elements attributed to the October 27, 1990 waiver really come from that one provision (Pub. L. 101-466), that the other October 1990 waiver is dated October 31 so the date disambiguates, that the November 20, 1995 waiver (Pub. L. 104-56) reaches a debt limit extension measure and names the Committee on House Oversight, that the U.S. Code note heading introduces the whole run rather than one entry, and - the crux - that no sentence now claims anything about the waiver practice as a whole beyond "repeatedly waived both sections outright". It also confirmed the two articles are word-for-word identical on the shared passage, so they cannot diverge in production. Two minor findings, both fixed after the pass and re-verified verbatim by a fresh source read in the main thread: "of that Congress" had no antecedent (the quotation now runs on to "of the One Hundred First Congress"), and this article had left a sourced frequency phrase unquoted where its sibling quoted it (now quoted in full). Both fixes are pure extensions of quotations the pass had already verified; they add no assertion.
claims.sourceSpan: any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill, or continuing resolution of the One Hundred First Congress

notes: First-refresh audit of the largest unaudited explainer on the site, Phase B House-procedure batch. Its opening sentence carried an invented statistic (5% / 95% of enacted legislation) that no stored source contains, and two absolute claims about committee and Rules Committee control that House Rule XV clause 2 refutes on its own terms and that the site’s own discharge-petition explainer already contradicted. The reconciliation section was rebuilt on CRS R48444, which the page had been citing without ever fetching: the "once per budget resolution" limit is wrong (up to three), and the list of reconciliation laws is now receipted to that report’s appendix and gains the FY2025 law (P.L. 119-21) that a site tracking the 119th Congress should not have been missing. Round A (fresh hostile Sonnet pass over the frozen draft, plus my own independent source read, run 2026-08-31 after the previous session died mid-verification and its unreported rounds were discarded under the GENUINE-READ rule) found three more material defects, all in the reconciliation section or its neighbourhood: the struck-short-title set was undercounted at two when CRS names three of this article’s own laws, the striking was attributed to the Byrd rule when the report attributes it to no rule at all, and the 20-hour debate limit was stated without the chamber the statute binds. A fourth, minor: an unsourced "the chair often sends the bill to a subcommittee first" that no ledger row covered and that CRS contradicts by saying the practice varies. A hostile sign-off round over the frozen file then PASSED all four fixes with source quoted, independently re-deriving the "three of those" arithmetic and confirming the 20-hour limit sits in the subsection headed "Procedure in Senate". It surfaced two further minor items, both fixed: an unsourced "how rarely that threshold is reached" deferred to another page, and a ledger-coverage gap on the two-phase sentence. Rounds C and D then ran as two independent fresh hostile passes. Round C was clean on every quotation, figure and receipt, and independently re-derived the struck-short-title arithmetic and the 102-public-law count. Round D, attacking the prose rather than the receipts, found the batch’s sharpest defect on the fifth pass: "Two limits do bind the contents" was a precise completeness claim that CRS R48444’s own question 5 refutes with four points of order, sorted by chamber. It also caught an absolute the sources do not support ("much of the Senate’s work never reaches that machinery") and three frequency words chosen by us rather than by CRS. A cross-batch handover from the veto cluster then corrected the pocket-veto reasoning: the article had given the 1929 dicta as the reason a pocket veto cannot be overridden, and CRS RL30909 both labels that point dicta and records the 1974 Vocational Rehabilitation Act override that contradicts it in practice.
